power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p<0.05", "p<0.05", "p<0.05", "p < 0.05", 
"p < 0.05", "p < 0.05", "p < 0.05", "p > 0.05", "p > 0.05"), 
    Text = c("The boy's account (9-12 years) was shown a significantly higher monthly frequency of child-targeted unhealthy food marketing instances (340, 70.2%) than the boy's account (5-8 years; 241, 66.2%), the girl's account (5-8 years; 261, 60.6%), the man's account (224, 57.7%), and the woman's account (263, 54.7%) during a 24-hour (p<0.05) but not a 2-hour daily viewing period.", 
    "Monthly frequencies of some core child-targeted techniques shown to the boy's account (9-12 years) were also higher than other accounts during a 24-hour (p<0.05) but not a 2-hour daily viewing period.", 
    "All analyses were performed in R (version 4.3.0) [33], with p<0.05 indicating statistically significant differences.", 
    "a Significantly different than the boy 9-12 years account (p < 0.05).", 
    "b Significantly different than the boy 5-8 years account (p < 0.05).", 
    "c Significantly different than the man's account (p < 0.05).", 
    "b Significantly different than the man's account (p < 0.05).", 
    "Under the first alternative definition which included core and broad child-targeted techniques, we found that the mean monthly frequency and proportion of childtargeted unhealthy food marketing were identical to results from our primary analyses (child accounts: 283, 94.0%; adult accounts: 243, 91.0%; p > 0.05).", 
    "However, under the second definition which included core, broad, and non-specific techniques, all unhealthy food marketing instances were classified as child-targeted (child accounts: 301, 100.0%; adult accounts: 267, 100.0%; p > 0.05)."
    )), row.names = c(NA, -9L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.title: Non-Significant P Value Check
stat_p_nonsig.summary_text: We found 2 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

table.formatted: Under the first alternative definition which included core and broad child-targeted techniques, we found that the mean monthly frequency and proportion of childtargeted unhealthy food marketing were identical to results from our primary analyses (child accounts: 283, 94.0%; adult accounts: 243, 91.0%; p > 0.05).

table.formatted: However, under the second definition which included core, broad, and non-specific techniques, all unhealthy food marketing instances were classified as child-targeted (child accounts: 301, 100.0%; adult accounts: 267, 100.0%; p > 0.05).
table.expanded: However, under the second definition which included core, broad, and non-specific techniques, all unhealthy food marketing instances were classified as child-targeted (child accounts: 301, 100.0%; adult accounts: 267, 100.0%; p > 0.05).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p > 0.05", "p > 0.05"), Sentence = c("Under the first alternative definition which included core and broad child-targeted techniques, we found that the mean monthly frequency and proportion of childtargeted unhealthy food marketing were identical to results from our primary analyses (child accounts: 283, 94.0%; adult accounts: 243, 91.0%; p > 0.05).", "However, under the second definition which included core, broad, and non-specific techniques, all unhealthy food marketing instances were classified as child-targeted (child accounts: 301, 100.0%; adult accounts: 267, 100.0%; p > 0.05)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::
